subject: Business Models
title: Birth of Freemium
description: A micro-lesson that makes Birth of Freemium usable.

hook.text: In 2006, venture capitalist Fred Wilson coined 'freemium'—combining free + premium into one business model.

buildup.text: The idea: give the basic product away for free, then charge power users for advanced features.

discovery.text: Freemium exploits near-zero marginal cost. Serving one more free user costs almost nothing in software.

twist.text: The concept predated the name. Shareware in the 1980s used the same idea: try it free, pay to keep it.

climax.text: Freemium became the dominant model for internet businesses. Free gets users. Premium gets revenue.

punchline.text: Free to start, pay to stay. Fred Wilson named what the internet already knew.

details.summary: The freemium model emerged in the early 2000s as software companies discovered they could acquire massive user bases by offering core products for free while charging for premium features..
details.whyItMatters: Freemium fundamentally changed how software businesses acquire customers. Instead of spending on marketing to convince people to buy, companies let the product sell itself through free usage.
takeaways: Free core products attract massive user bases with minimal marketing spend
A small percentage of users convert to paid, funding the entire operation
Fred Wilson coined the term 'freemium' in 2006 to describe this model

faq.question: What was the first successful freemium software product?
faq.answer: While shareware pioneered the concept in the 1980s, Skype in 2003 was among the first major freemium successes in the modern era. Free voice calls attracted millions of users, and paid features like calling landlines generated revenue from a small converting percentage.

faq.question: Why did freemium become dominant after 2000 rather than earlier?
faq.answer: Broadband internet enabled free distribution at near-zero cost. Cloud computing eliminated the need for users to install software. Viral sharing features amplified organic growth. Venture capital funded the gap between free user acquisition and eventual monetization.
